main.title: Alien vs Predator
main.subtitle: Three ways into the same nightmare
main.summary: Alien vs Predator is Rebellion's first-person game for the Atari Jaguar, released in October 1994.

cards.heading: Three ways into the same nightmare
cards.text: Alien vs Predator is Rebellion's first-person game for the Atari Jaguar, released in October 1994. Its three scenarios place an Alien, a Predator or a Colonial Marine inside the infested Golgotha base. The same corridors support different objectives and abilities, changing the meaning of an encounter according to the creature being controlled. The base connects five levels through elevators and air ducts, creating a place to learn and navigate while its inhabitants turn every journey between rooms into a threat.

cards.heading: A marine searching for an escape
cards.text: As Marine Lance J. Lewis, the player begins without weapons or security clearance and must assemble the means to escape. Fallen soldiers provide guns, ammunition and access cards, while terminals reveal information about the base. The motion tracker becomes another tool for reading dangers beyond the immediate view. Reaching the self-destruct mechanism and finding an escape pod gives exploration a practical purpose. Each newly opened door may advance that plan, but also increases the area in which supplies and a safe route must be remembered.

cards.heading: Hunting by another set of rules
cards.text: The Alien travels through air ducts and fights with claws, jaw and tail. It prepares future bodies by infecting Marines, turning a successful attack into a possible return after death. The Predator instead hunts for the Alien queen's skull and gains weapons through an honor-based score: killing while invisible can cost progress. Its camouflage and vision filters offer different ways to read a room. These changes extend beyond the appearance of the weapon, making each scenario a distinct relationship with the same hostile architecture.

main.title: Super Punch-Out!!
main.subtitle: Read the boxer in front
main.summary: Super Punch-Out!! is Nintendo’s Super Nintendo boxing game, viewed from behind a translucent player character. The opponent fills the space ahead, making every shift of guard or preparation for a punch easy to study. The player works toward the World Video Boxing Association championship through a cast of exaggerated fighters. A bout must be won within three minutes, turning observation into an urgent task. The challenge is to recognise an opponent’s habits, defend against the next attack and find the opening that follows.

cards.heading: Read the boxer in front
cards.text: Super Punch-Out!! is Nintendo’s Super Nintendo boxing game, viewed from behind a translucent player character. The opponent fills the space ahead, making every shift of guard or preparation for a punch easy to study. The player works toward the World Video Boxing Association championship through a cast of exaggerated fighters. A bout must be won within three minutes, turning observation into an urgent task. The challenge is to recognise an opponent’s habits, defend against the next attack and find the opening that follows.

cards.heading: A gap in the guard
cards.text: Jabs and body blows can be aimed from either hand, while blocks, dodges and ducks provide different ways to avoid an incoming strike. An opponent’s raised gloves identify where a punch is likely to be stopped, so aiming and timing matter together. Repeatedly attacking the same defended area wastes an opportunity and invites retaliation. The view makes the exchange almost a conversation of gestures: a movement offers a clue, the player chooses a response, and a successful answer creates room for the next punch.

cards.heading: Winning is only the beginning
cards.text: An opponent who first seems overwhelming becomes more manageable once the player recognises the order and timing of the attacks. That makes another attempt useful even after the general controls are familiar. The three-minute limit encourages a sharper performance, with fewer wasted punches and quicker use of an exposed guard. Super Punch-Out!! carries the series’ arcade emphasis on recognisable personalities and precise responses onto the Super Nintendo, using detailed animation and the transparent viewpoint to keep the information for each exchange directly in front of the player.

main.title: Samurai Shodown II
main.subtitle: Another meeting of blades
main.summary: Samurai Shodown II is SNK's weapon-based fighting game, first released for Neo Geo in October 1994.

cards.heading: Another meeting of blades
cards.text: Samurai Shodown II is SNK's weapon-based fighting game, first released for Neo Geo in October 1994. Haohmaru and most of the original cast return alongside new fighters as Mizuki Rashojin becomes the central threat. The large weapons make distance and the timing of a single opening important, with the expanded movement system providing more ways to manage that space. The sequel refines the original's dramatic exchanges while giving players additional answers to attacks, so waiting within striking range becomes a more active contest of observation and response.

cards.heading: A movement that saves the round
cards.text: Characters can roll forward or backwards, duck under high attacks and make small hops over low ones. A defensive command performed at the right moment can deflect an incoming strike and briefly expose the opponent. These options give particular attacks particular answers, encouraging the player to recognise their height and timing. A large swing may still promise substantial damage, but a prepared rival has another way to escape it or turn it aside. The encounter becomes a sequence of commitments, with each successful defensive movement creating a possible reply.

cards.heading: The danger of losing a weapon
cards.text: The POW meter now supports powerful special techniques that can break an opponent's weapon. Fighting without that weapon changes the immediate balance until a replacement arrives, making the successful attack a disruption as well as a loss of health. Character-specific moves, hidden encounters and small appearances by other SNK figures add further reasons to explore the cast. The sequel's improvements serve its central spectacle: two armed fighters can produce a decisive exchange in a moment, and the expanded systems give both players more influence over how that moment is reached.

main.title: Killer Instinct
main.summary: Killer Instinct is a 1994 fighting game developed by Rare and first published for arcades by Midway.

cards.heading: Killer Instinct reaches the arcade
cards.text: Killer Instinct is a 1994 fighting game developed by Rare and published by Midway for arcades in October 1994. Nintendo published versions for both the Super Nintendo Entertainment System and the Game Boy the following year. The game's plot involves an all-powerful corporation organizing a fighting tournament. The story was adapted in a limited comic book series published under the short-lived Acclaim Comics imprint.

cards.heading: Planning a new fighting game
cards.text: According to Ken Lobb, during his time at Namco Hometek, the groundwork for Killer Instinct started as a Namco's fighting game project in the early planning stages, titled Melee (which itself later became WeaponLord). Aspects of Killer Instinct's core gameplay were influenced from SNK fighting games, namely both the World Heroes and the Fatal Fury series, particularly the characters Kim Dragon and Kim Kaphwan.

cards.heading: Life bars, doubles and breakers
cards.text: Killer Instinct combined detailed graphics and a varied cast with a fighting system built around long combos and ways to interrupt them. Instead of fighting enemies in best-of-three-rounds bouts, each player has two life bars. The player that depletes the other player's life bars first wins the match. The game also introduced "auto-doubles", a feature which allows players to press a certain sequence of buttons to make characters automatically perform combos on opponents. Also featured in the game are "combo breakers", special defensive moves that can interrupt combos.

cards.heading: Conversions and a continuing series
cards.text: A critical and commercial success, Killer Instinct was followed by a sequel, the 1996 arcade game Killer Instinct 2, later ported to the Nintendo 64 as Killer Instinct Gold. After Microsoft acquired the franchise alongside developer Rare, a new 2013 game rebooting the franchise was released, serving as a launch title for the Xbox One. An emulated version of the original game is included with the 2013 game, under the title Killer Instinct Classic. The SNES version of the game was re-released on the Nintendo Classics service on February 21, 2024. Retrospective lists by various publications included it among the best fighting games of all time.

main.title: Sonic the Hedgehog: Triple Trouble
main.subtitle: Three rivals for the emeralds
main.summary: Sonic the Hedgehog: Triple Trouble is Aspect's platform game, first released for Game Gear in Japan on 11 November 1994.

cards.heading: Three rivals for the emeralds
cards.text: Sonic the Hedgehog: Triple Trouble is Aspect's platform game, first released for Game Gear in Japan on 11 November 1994. Sonic and Tails try to protect the Chaos Emeralds from Doctor Robotnik, Knuckles and the treasure hunter Fang, known internationally as Nack. Six zones carry the adventure through familiar running, jumping and boss encounters, with a choice between the two heroes. The handheld sequel builds on Sonic Chaos while giving each protagonist particular movement and equipment, allowing the same overall journey to produce different opportunities inside its stages.

cards.heading: Two heroes through six zones
cards.text: Both Sonic and Tails can use a spin dash to accelerate from a stationary roll. Sonic also has the peel-out move associated with Sonic CD, while Tails can fly for a limited time. Those abilities encourage different approaches to platforms and gaps: a useful run-up may favour Sonic, while an elevated opening can reward Tails' flight. Each zone ends with a boss after its opening stages, giving the route a repeated progression from learning the environment to facing a more concentrated mechanical challenge at the end.

cards.heading: Equipment for another way across
cards.text: Some power-ups belong to only one hero, including Sonic's jet board and equipment for Tails' underwater travel. Collecting them can change how a section is crossed, making the choice of character visible in the route as well as the animation. Yayoi Fujimori composed the music. Fang's introduction also added another recurring face to the wider series. Triple Trouble gives the Game Gear its own substantial Sonic journey, using the two heroes' abilities and colourful stages to bring the handheld adventure closer to the variety associated with the larger console games.

main.title: Warcraft: Orcs & Humans
main.summary: Warcraft: Orcs & Humans is a real-time strategy game (RTS) developed and published by Blizzard Entertainment, and published by Interplay Productions in Europe.

cards.heading: Warcraft: Orcs & Humans
cards.text: Warcraft: Orcs & Humans is a real-time strategy game (RTS) developed and published by Blizzard Entertainment, and published by Interplay Productions in Europe. It was released for MS-DOS in North America on November 15, 1994, and for Mac OS in early 1996. The MS-DOS version was re-released by Sold-Out Software in 2002. It is the first game in the Warcraft fantasy game franchise.

cards.heading: Multiplayer reshapes real-time strategy
cards.text: Warcraft: Orcs & Humans helped establish multiplayer as an expectation for real-time strategy games. Its mission design and other gameplay elements also influenced subsequent RTS developers, alongside the small-force management and fantasy setting that would distinguish the series.

cards.heading: Reception and legacy
cards.text: Warcraft games emphasize skillful management of relatively small forces, and they maintain characters and storylines within a cohesive fictional universe. Sales were fairly high, reviewers were mostly impressed, and the game won three awards and was a finalist for three others. The game's sequel, Warcraft II: Tides of Darkness, became the main rival to the Command & Conquer series by Westwood Studios. This competition fostered an "RTS boom" in the mid– to late 1990s.

main.title: Hagane: The Final Conflict
main.subtitle: CAProduction / Red Entertainment · Super Nintendo Entertainment System
main.summary: Hagane: The Final Conflict is a Super Nintendo action platformer about a surviving ninja restored through cybernetic technology. Hagane pursues the faction that destroyed his clan, crossing a world where traditional armour and supernatural imagery meet futuristic machinery. Keita Amemiya's designs give the warrior a particularly elaborate silhouette. The player receives a broad range of attacks and movements from the beginning, making the task one of learning how to use an already capable body rather than waiting for a long sequence of abilities to become available.

cards.heading: A ninja rebuilt for revenge
cards.text: Hagane: The Final Conflict is a Super Nintendo action platformer about a surviving ninja restored through cybernetic technology. Hagane pursues the faction that destroyed his clan, crossing a world where traditional armour and supernatural imagery meet futuristic machinery. Keita Amemiya's designs give the warrior a particularly elaborate silhouette. The player receives a broad range of attacks and movements from the beginning, making the task one of learning how to use an already capable body rather than waiting for a long sequence of abilities to become available.

cards.heading: Choose a movement as carefully as a weapon
cards.text: A sword, chain, shuriken and grenades offer different ways to reach an opponent. Wall jumps, slides, somersaults and aerial attacks expand the routes through a dangerous section, while limited magic supplies a stronger intervention. Each ability has a practical relationship to distance and position. The player needs to recognise whether an enemy is best approached, attacked from farther away or passed with a movement that leaves room for another threat. The large move set rewards deliberate choices once the immediate controls become familiar.

cards.heading: Short stages, demanding execution
cards.text: Most stages concentrate their hazards into relatively short stretches with few checkpoints, making a mistake costly despite the hero's powerful abilities. A hovercraft sequence changes the perspective through the console's Mode 7 effects. Published by Hudson Soft in Japan in 1994, the game reached Europe and North America in 1995. Its distinctive visual mixture supports the same idea as its controls: a traditional ninja has acquired another kind of body, and the challenge is to understand the precise possibilities that body brings into the fight.

main.title: Donkey Kong Country
main.summary: Donkey Kong Country, known in Japan as Super Donkey Kong, is a 1994 platform game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).

cards.heading: Donkey Kong and Diddy reclaim the hoard
cards.text: Donkey Kong Country, known in Japan as Super Donkey Kong, is a 1994 platform game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES). It follows the gorilla Donkey Kong and his nephew Diddy Kong as they set out to recover their stolen banana hoard from the crocodile King K. Rool and his army, the Kremlings. The player traverses 40 side-scrolling levels as they jump between platforms and avoid obstacles. They collect items, ride minecarts and animals, defeat enemies and bosses, and find secret bonus stages. In multiplayer modes, two players work cooperatively or race.

cards.heading: Rare brings rendered graphics to SNES
cards.text: After developing Nintendo Entertainment System games in the 1980s, Rare, a British studio founded by Tim and Chris Stamper, purchased Silicon Graphics workstations to render 3D models. Nintendo sought a game to compete with Sega's Aladdin (1993) and commissioned Rare to reboot the dormant Donkey Kong franchise. Rare assembled 12 developers to work on Donkey Kong Country over 18 months. Donkey Kong Country was inspired by the Super Mario series and was one of the first home console games to feature pre-rendered graphics, achieved through a compression technique that converted 3D models into SNES sprites with little loss of detail. It was the first Donkey Kong game neither produced nor directed by the franchise's creator, Shigeru Miyamoto, though he contributed design ideas.

cards.heading: A major campaign and a major success
cards.text: Following its announcement at the Consumer Electronics Show in June 1994, Donkey Kong Country was highly anticipated and backed by a large marketing campaign that cost $16 million in America alone. It was released in November 1994 to acclaim; critics hailed its visuals as groundbreaking and praised its gameplay and music. Its quality and design were favourably compared to the Super Mario series. Donkey Kong Country received several year-end accolades and set the record for the fastest-selling video game at the time. With 9.3 million copies sold worldwide, it is the third-bestselling SNES game and the bestselling Donkey Kong game. Following the success, Nintendo purchased a large minority stake in Rare, which became a prominent second-party developer for Nintendo during the late 1990s.

cards.heading: An adventure that keeps returning
cards.text: Donkey Kong Country re-established Donkey Kong as a major Nintendo franchise and helped maintain the SNES's popularity into the fifth generation of video game consoles. Journalists regard it as one of the greatest video games, although its pre-rendered visuals became divisive. Nintendo rereleased Donkey Kong Country on the Game Boy Color, Game Boy Advance, and digital distribution services. Rare followed it with the SNES games Donkey Kong Country 2: Diddy's Kong Quest (1995) and Donkey Kong Country 3: Dixie Kong's Double Trouble! (1996), and the Nintendo 64 game Donkey Kong 64 (1999). After a hiatus, during which Rare was acquired by the Nintendo competitor Microsoft, Retro Studios revived the series with Donkey Kong Country Returns (2010) for the Wii and Donkey Kong Country: Tropical Freeze (2014) for the Wii U.

features.title: David Wise: composing within memory limits
features.summary: A soundtrack takes shape through programming.

cards.heading: A demo might be replaced
cards.text: David Wise recalled initially expecting Nintendo to replace his Donkey Kong Country demos with an in-house composer's work. The early jungle pieces remained in the game, and his contribution grew from there. His recollection describes a score developed through drafts, selection and approval during production, before its later reputation was established.

cards.heading: Small waves make a current
cards.text: For Aquatic Ambience, Wise wanted a sound behaviour he associated with the Korg Wavestation. He recalled spending five weeks, much of it on technical work, arranging small waveforms in different orders. Changing the sequence changed the timbre while conserving memory. Building those sounds was part of composing the underwater piece: its texture depended on how the instrument had been programmed.

cards.heading: Edit, assemble, listen again
cards.text: Wise described editing and assembly as recurring parts of composition. On the NES he had entered hexadecimal subroutines in the Brief editor; for the SNES he again chose to code because memory was limited. He could repeat the edit, assemble and listen cycle hundreds of times as a tune developed, testing each small change through playback.

cards.heading: Make room for the world
cards.text: Rare involved music early in development. Wise recalled that Nintendo gave first drafts room before proposing changes. When separate sound channels were scarce, he sometimes incorporated environmental sounds into the music, placing them rhythmically. Composition therefore involved sharing the available resources with sound effects and responding to changes in the game being built around the score.

main.title: Sega Saturn
main.subtitle: The arcade has more than one future
main.summary: Saturn brought Sega's arcade ambitions home while giving richly drawn 2D games a place beside the new polygon worlds.

cards.heading: Virtua Fighter reaches the home
cards.text: Sega Saturn launched in Japan on 22 November 1994 with Virtua Fighter among its defining attractions. Sega's arcade fighting game had made three-dimensional characters a compelling new spectacle. Bringing that kind of experience into the home became one of the machine's central promises.

cards.heading: More than polygon graphics
cards.text: Saturn's library also became a home for 2D fighting games and shooters, supported in some cases by additional memory cartridges. Sega's own retrospective places those games alongside arcade adaptations such as Daytona USA, Sega Rally Championship and Virtua Fighter 2. The new generation could develop several visual languages at once.

cards.heading: The western launch
cards.text: The platform reached North America in 1995, in a market where Sega was also trying to extend the life of Genesis through the 32 X. Those overlapping plans made the transition complicated. The grey Japanese launch machine and black western versions also remind us that Saturn was never encountered in exactly the same way everywhere: its hardware, software library and position in the market depended on where a player lived.

cards.heading: The surprise at E3
cards.text: On May 11, 1995, during the first E3, Sega announced that Saturn was already available through selected North American retailers. The launch arrived months ahead of the previously communicated plan and attempted to seize space before PlayStation. The decision became one of the most discussed commercial episodes in console history: it created a time advantage but put pressure on distribution, developers and retailer relationships. Saturn was also a technically unusual machine, powerful in 2D and complex to exploit for 3D.

cards.heading: Supporting an early launch
cards.text: Sega had announced a September launch in the United States. At the E3 keynote on May 11, 1995, Tom Kalinske instead revealed that Saturn was available immediately through selected retailers. Limited quantities, a restricted retail network and an incomplete software lineup complicated that early start. Shops and developers had prepared for a different schedule, making the surprise launch difficult to support consistently.

cards.heading: Two SH-2 processors
cards.text: Saturn combined two SH-2 CPUs with dedicated processors for graphics, sound and other tasks. Using them effectively required developers to divide work carefully between components. Its parallel architecture offered considerable capability, but the complexity of the hardware and tools made rapid development difficult. Teams needed detailed knowledge of how the processors cooperated to get the most from the machine.

cards.heading: From Model 1 to the living room
cards.text: Sega brought a strong arcade library to Saturn. Virtua Fighter, originally built for the Model 1 arcade hardware, was a particularly visible demonstration of polygonal fighting at home. Other Sega titles benefited from the similarities between Saturn and the ST-V arcade board. These conversions connected the console to Sega's arcade identity, while requiring teams to adapt timing, animation and controls for home play.

features.title: Saturn's different clocks
features.summary: Sega veterans recalled the different technical and commercial challenges of Saturn.

cards.heading: Keeping what the team knew
cards.text: Hideki Sato recalled developing Saturn during the transition from sprites to polygon graphics. Sega already had considerable experience and software built around two-dimensional games. His team chose to support both approaches as the company's arcade work demonstrated the possibilities of 3D. The design therefore reflected Sega's existing skills as well as its plans for a new generation.

cards.heading: Tools between a chip and a game
cards.text: Sato acknowledged that Saturn's software libraries were insufficient for outside developers. The architecture could be difficult to use, and third parties needed better tools and support. In his retrospective, he also contrasted the machine's Japanese sales with its struggles overseas. His account links the hardware design to the practical work of helping other studios produce games for it.

cards.heading: An announcement reaches the shops
cards.text: Interviewed in 2015, Tom Kalinske argued that Saturn's surprise North American launch should have waited for a fuller software lineup, the participation of all retailers and broader marketing. From Sega of America's perspective, getting consoles onto some shelves early had left other parts of the launch unprepared. Retailers, developers and customers had been working toward a later date.

cards.heading: A plan remembered afterwards
cards.text: Kalinske also described the audience he would have targeted: college-age and older players, with younger customers drawn toward the games they played. His recollections focus on retail, marketing and launch timing, while Sato's account concentrates on development knowledge and tools. Together they describe several decisions that shaped Saturn's different fortunes in Japan and overseas.

main.title: The Need for Speed
main.summary: Road & Track Presents: The Need for Speed (also known simply as The Need for Speed) is a 1994 racing game developed by EA Canada and Pioneer Productions and published by Electronic Arts for 3DO. Versions with additional tracks were released for MS-DOS (1995), PlayStation (1996), and Saturn (1996). The 1996 Windows release is subtitled SE (Special Edition).

cards.heading: The first Need for Speed
cards.text: Road & Track Presents: The Need for Speed (also known simply as The Need for Speed) is a 1994 racing game developed by EA Canada and Pioneer Productions and published by Electronic Arts for 3DO. Versions with additional tracks were released for MS-DOS (1995), PlayStation (1996), and Saturn (1996). The 1996 Windows release is subtitled SE (Special Edition).

cards.heading: Open roads, traffic and police
cards.text: The original 3DO version offers three point-to-point routes, each divided into three stages. Later ports add closed circuits, with three additional tracks on PlayStation and Saturn. Traffic and police give the open roads another source of risk: being caught repeatedly can end the race. The Special Edition also rewards tournament victories with the Lost Vegas track, a fictional jet-powered Warrior PTO E/2 and further modes that change car handling or mirror the courses.

cards.heading: Car profiles and saved replays
cards.text: The licensed cars have detailed specifications, histories, audio commentaries and real-life video clips. These profiles present the vehicles as objects to examine as well as machines to race. Saved replays offer multiple camera views, playback speeds and navigation controls so players can watch a race again.

cards.heading: Road & Track brings the cars to life
cards.text: The Need for Speed was noted for its realism and audio and video commentaries. Electronic Arts collaborated with automotive magazine Road & Track to match vehicle behaviour, including the mimicking of the sounds made by the vehicles' gear control levers. The game also contained precise vehicle data with commentary, several "magazine-style" images of each car's interior and exterior and short video clips highlighting the vehicles set to music. Inspiration for the gameplay came from Test Drive, which had shared development staff with The Need for Speed. The Need for Speed was released in 1994 for 3DO consoles.

cards.heading: Over Drivin' and its Japanese editions
cards.text: In 1994, Electronic Arts Victor translated the 3DO version of The Need for Speed into Japanese, and released it in Japan as Road & Track Presents: OverDrivin'. The PlayStation port of the game was exported to that country as Over Drivin' DX in 1996. Two additional Nissan-sponsored versions of the game were announced at that year's Tokyo Game Show: Nissan Presents: Over Drivin' GT-R (released in 1996 for the Sega Saturn) and Nissan Presents: Over Drivin' Skyline Memorial (released in 1997 for the PlayStation). The former's car lineup consists only of Nissan vehicles, whilst the latter exclusively features Skyline models.
